'''Taner Edis''' (born August 20, 1967) is a [[Turkish Americans|Turkish American]] physicist and [[Scientific skepticism|skeptic]].  He is a professor of physics at [[Truman State University]].<ref name=nyt2009/> He received his B.S. from [[Boğaziçi University]] in Turkey and his M.A. and [[Doctor of Philosophy|Ph.D.]] from [[Johns Hopkins University]].<ref>{{cite web|title=Curriculum Vitae: Taner Edis|url=http://edis.sites.truman.edu/cv/cv/|website=[[Truman State University]]|access-date=April 26, 2016}}</ref> Edis is the author of several books on creationism, religion and science. He is a fellow for the [[Committee for Skeptical Inquiry]].

==Early life==

Born in [[Istanbul, Turkey]] to secular Turkish and American parents, Edis traveled to the United States many times in his childhood.<ref name="PoI 2007"/><ref name=nyt2007>{{cite news |title=Islamic Creationist and a Book Sent Round the World |newspaper=New York Times |author=Cornelia Dean |date=7 July 2007 |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2007/07/17/science/17book.html}}</ref>

Edis has lived in the United States since starting his master's degree at [[Johns Hopkins University]]. He earned his Ph.D. in 1994.<ref name=nyt2007/> He first encountered [[creationism]] during his studies in America&nbsp;&ndash; he thought it an "American oddity".<ref name=nyt2009>{{cite news |newspaper=New York Times |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2009/11/03/science/03islam.html |title=Creationism, Minus a Young Earth, Emerges in the Islamic World |date=2 November 2009 |author=Kenneth Chang}}</ref>

==Career==

Edis is professor of physics at Truman State University.<ref name=nyt2009/> He became a fellow for [[Committee for Skeptical Inquiry]] in 2022.<ref>{{cite journal |title=Committee for Skeptical Inquiry Elects 14 New Fellows from Six Countries |journal=Skeptical Inquirer |date=2022 |volume=46 |issue=2 |pages=7–10}}</ref>

==Skepticism==

Edis's research "focuses on paranormal and supernatural claims and explores what their failures say about the nature of science". He is particularly interested in Islamic [[creationism]] and the American [[intelligent design]] movement.<ref name=mcb>{{cite book |editor=C. Mackenzie Brown |title=Asian Religious Responses to Darwinism: Evolutionary Theories in Middle Eastern, South Asian, and East Asian Cultural Contexts |publisher=Springer |year=2020 |page=36 |isbn=9783030373405}}</ref> Edis has been called "a liberal atheist, secular humanist and a zealous proselyte of scientific reason".<ref name=dunn/>

Fascinated by the plethora of supernatural and fringe science beliefs around him, and concerned about the rise of Islamist politics back in Turkey, Edis first got involved with skeptical inquiry into religious and paranormal claims during his graduate studies. "Science is difficult," states Edis to [[Point of Inquiry]] interviewer [[D.J. Grothe]] in answer to a question about why science has not replaced religion. Edis explains to his students that they will have difficulty understanding this "because the human brain is not wired to understand something like quantum mechanics and neutrinos correctly, it's a struggle."<ref name="PoI 2008">{{cite web|last1=Grothe|first1=D.J.|author-link=D.J. Grothe|title=Taner Edis - Science and Nonbelief|url=http://www.pointofinquiry.org/taner_edis_science_and_nonbelief/|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170505042603/https://pointofinquiry.org/taner_edis_science_and_nonbelief|archive-date=May 5, 2017|website=Point of Inquiry|publisher=Center for Inquiry|date=June 6, 2008}}</ref> In an interview with [[Susan Gerbic]] at [[CSICon]], Edis characterized his more recent writings on the subjects of science and skepticism by saying that "it might [even] be rational to believe in certain falsehoods. The argument turns on the costs of acquiring and possessing beliefs; sometimes truth is just too costly."<ref name=GerbicMisinformation17/>

Edis has given several lectures about Islamic creationism. One of his premises is that creationism in the United States is quite moderate compared to Islamic countries. Turkey for example, despite being known as a secular state, has high levels of belief in a young Earth. This is because the textbooks and curriculum in the schools do not offer both evolution and creationism, but only creationism. Teaching evolution is not part of the syllabus at all.<ref>{{cite web|title=Ehab Abouheif & Taner Edis on Evolution and Islam|url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=RS7mPtsfejg|website=TV Islam Science| date=August 18, 2014 |publisher=Hampshire College|access-date=23 April 2016}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|last1=Edis|first1=Taner|title=Taner Edis Reasonfest 2013|date=June 26, 2013 |url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=i6lY78CUS8g|publisher=Reason Fest 2013|access-date=23 April 2016}}</ref><ref name=GerbicMisinformation17>{{cite web|last1=Gerbic|first1=Susan|author-link=Susan Gerbic|title=The Age of Misinformation is More Global Than We Might Think|url=https://www.csicop.org/specialarticles/show/the_age_of_misinformation_is_more_global_than_we_might_think|website=Skeptical Inquiry|date=July 31, 2017 |publisher=Committee For Skeptical Inquiry|access-date=7 November 2017|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170731165517/https://www.csicop.org/specialarticles/show/the_age_of_misinformation_is_more_global_than_we_might_think|archive-date=31 July 2017}}</ref> Grothe asked Taner in 2007 if he thought that Islam could be compatible with western science. His answer was that it just depends on the type of Islam. As in Christianity there are both liberal and conservative Muslims. The more liberal their views the more compatible they are with science.<ref name="PoI 2007">{{cite web|last1=Grothe|first1=D.J.|author-link=D.J. Grothe|title=Taner Edis - Science and Religion in Islam|url=http://www.pointofinquiry.org/taner_edis_science_and_religion_in_islam/|website=Point of Inquiry|date=April 27, 2007 |publisher=Center for Inquiry|access-date=23 April 2016}}</ref>

Concerning [[crop circles]] Edis wrote that we know how these are created, we know the techniques. "So we do not need to find the perpetrator of every crop circle to figure out that probably they all are human made. Many true believers remain who continue to think there is something paranormal — perhaps alien — about crop circles. But the circles we know all fall within the range of the sort of thing done in hoaxes. Nothing stands out as extraordinary."<ref>{{cite book|last1=Edis|first1=Taner|title=Science and Nonbelief|date=2008|publisher=Prometheus Books|isbn=978-1-59102-561-0|page=138}}</ref>

{{Cquote|One thing I think we need to be more impressed with, is how naturally religion comes to a normal human mind. ... It is not so much death of perception of supernatural agents all around us, it's that organized religion has lost its ability to convince people. That's very different than people becoming science-minded skeptics and rationalists... it's religion fading away that is the default."<ref name="PoI 2008"/>}}

==Reception==

Edis was an editor of the book ''Why Intelligent Design Fails'', which has received positive reviews.<ref>Menuge, Angus J. L. (2008). ''Reviewed Work: Why Intelligent Design Fails: A Scientific Critique of the New Creationism by Matt Young, Taner Edis''. ''[[Politics and the Life Sciences]]''. Vol. 27, No. 2 pp. 52-54.</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Sepkoski |first1=David |title=Worldviews in Collision: Recent Literature on the Creation–Evolution Divide |journal=[[Journal of the History of Biology]] |date=2006 |volume=39 |issue=3 |pages=607–635 |doi=10.1007/s10739-006-9000-0|jstor=4332034|s2cid=83655972 }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Pigliucci |first1=Massimo |title=More than You Ever Wanted to Know about Intelligent Design|journal=[[Evolution (journal)|Evolution]]|date=2005 |volume=59 |issue=12 |pages=2717–2720 |doi=10.1111/j.0014-3820.2005.tb00983.x|jstor=3449064|doi-access=free }}</ref> His book ''The Ghost in the Universe'' received the Morris D. Forkosch Book Award for "Best Humanist Book of 2002"<ref>{{cite web|title=Forkosch Awards|url=https://www.secularhumanism.org/index.php/1180|website=[[Council for Secular Humanism]]|access-date=April 26, 2016}}</ref>

Reviewing Edis's 2016 book, ''Islam evolving: radicalism, reformation, and the uneasy relationship with the secular West'', J.P. Dunn writes that Edis gives a wide-ranging exposition of how the [[Qur'an]] has been variously interpreted to provide an alternative to Western beliefs, and that this will "challenge, offend, and enlighten" the book's readers.<ref name=dunn>{{cite journal |journal=Choice: Current Reviews for Academic Libraries |volume=54 |issue=3 |publisher=American Library Association |vauthors=Dunn, JP |year=2016 |title=Islam evolving: radicalism, reformation, and the uneasy relationship with the secular West |type=Book review}}</ref>

Within the context of Islam and science, Algerian astrophysicist [[Nidhal Guessoum]] categorizes Edis as a kind of "anti-harmonizer", who rejects the possibility that the two systems are reconciled. Guessoum writes that while Edis acknowledges that modern thinkers within Islam do not fully embrace anti-scientific religious dogmas, Edis is also "unhappy" that the materialist nature of science is not fully embraced.<ref name=guessoum>{{cite journal | last1 = Guessoum | first1 = Nidhal | title = Islam And Science: The Next Phase Of Debates | journal = Zygon | year=2015 | volume = 50 | issue = 4 | pages = 854–876 | issn = 0591-2385 | doi = 10.1111/zygo.12213 | pmid = | url = | doi-access = free }}</ref>

Philosopher [[John Gray (philosopher)|John Gray]] reviewed Edis's 2006 book, ''An Illusion of Harmony: Science and religion in Islam'' for ''[[The New Scientist]]''. Gray writes that Edis's thesis is that there is a fundamental incompatibility between Islam and science because of the religion's dogmatic precepts. Gray calls Edis's work "one of the few recent books that truly illuminates the troubled relationship between science and religion".<ref name=gray>{{cite journal |vauthors= Gray J |journal=[[New Scientist]] |title=Different faith, same struggle |year=2007 |volume=193 |issue=2592 |page=50 |doi=10.1016/S0262-4079(07)60486-2 |type=Book review}}</ref>
